CVE-2012-2763

[Mandatory] Title: CVE-2012-2763 / CWE-120: Buffer overflow in atom2str

[Optional] Disclosure / Patch Dates:
NA

NA

The Vulnerability
[Optional] CWE/CVE Number and description:
CWE-120: Buffer Copy without Checking Size of Input ('Classic Buffer Overflow')
[Mandatory] Summary:
A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the `atom2str` function within `plug-ins/script-fu/tinyscheme/scheme.c`. The flaw is triggered when the function processes specific character types, such as the DEL character (ASCII 127) or other control characters. In these cases, the code uses unsafe `strcpy` and `strcat` operations to write to a fixed-size buffer (`sc->strbuff`) without performing bounds checks, which can lead to a heap-based buffer overflow.
[Mandatory] Root cause:
Unchecked buffer length during string concatenation using `strcpy` and `strcat`.
[Mandatory] Attack Surface:
GIMP Script-Fu script interpreter
[Mandatory] Impact Summary:
Remote Code Execution
[Optional] Trigger / Attack vector:
Malicious Script-Fu script containing specific control characters.
[Mandatory] Key code/struct excerpt (minimal):
#if USE_ASCII_NAMES
     if(c==127) {
          strcpy(p,"#\\del"); break;
     } else if(c<32) {
          strcpy(p,"#\\"); strcat(p,charnames[c]); break;
     }
#else
     if(c<32) {
       sprintf(p,"#\\x%x",c); break;
     }
#endif

Exploit:

[Mandatory] Trigger surface/attack vector:
Malicious Script-Fu script processed by GIMP.

[Mandatory] Exploit primitive(s) available:
Heap buffer overflow (potential write-what-where).

[Mandatory] Exploitability summary (1 sentence):
The overflow is likely exploitable for remote code execution if an attacker can control the script input, though mitigations like heap canaries or ASLR may increase difficulty.

[Mandatory] Exploit script (summary, 3—6 bullets):
- Attacker crafts a Script-Fu script containing an object that resolves to a control character (e.g., ASCII 127).
- The script is loaded and executed by GIMP.
- GIMP's Script-Fu interpreter calls `atom2str` on the malicious object.
- The `strcpy`/`strcat` functions overflow the `sc->strbuff` buffer on the heap.
- This can corrupt heap metadata, potentially leading to arbitrary code execution.

Fix
[Mandatory] Fix code:
#if USE_ASCII_NAMES
     if(c==127) {
          snprintf(p,STRBUFFSIZE, "#\\del");
          break;
     } else if(c<32) {
          snprintf(p,STRBUFFSIZE, "#\\%s", charnames[c]);
          break;
     }
#else
     if(c<32) {
       sprintf(p,"#\\x%x",c); break;
     }
#endif

[Mandatory] Fix summary:
The patch replaces unsafe `strcpy` and `strcat` calls with `snprintf` to ensure that writes to the destination buffer are bounded by its size (`STRBUFFSIZE`), preventing the buffer overflow.

[Optional] Patch reference:
Commit 744f7a4a2b5acb8b531a6f5dd8744ebb95348fc2 in GNOME/gimp repository.

[Optional] Patch Analysis:
What did the fix do?
- Field: PatchType (bounds check added)
[Optional] Variant & Triage Guidance

[Optional] Variant analysis suggestions (2—3 bullets):
- Audit the entire `tinyscheme/scheme.c` file for other instances of unsafe string handling functions like `strcpy`, `strcat`, and `sprintf`.
- Review all functions that convert internal data types to string representations for similar buffer overflow risks.
- Fuzz the Script-Fu interpreter with maliciously crafted scripts containing long strings and special characters to uncover latent bugs.

CVE-2012-1571

[Mandatory] Title: CVE-2012-1571 / CWE-119:
Bounds check missing

[Optional] Disclosure / Patch Dates:
Initial advisory: NA — Patch release: NA

The Vulnerability
[Optional] CWE/CVE Number and description:
 Improper Restriction of Operations within the Bounds of a Memory Buffer
[Mandatory] Summary:
 The vulnerability is in the `cdf_read_property_info` function in `src/cdf.c`. When processing property information for a CDF_LENGTH32_STRING or CDF_LENGTH32_WSTRING type within a loop, the code calculates a new offset `o` but fails to verify that the resulting pointer `q + o` is still within the valid buffer boundary `e`. This allows an out-of-bounds read, which can be triggered by a specially crafted file.
[Mandatory] Root cause:
 Missing bounds check on the calculated pointer `q + o` before it is used within a loop.
[Mandatory] Attack Surface:
File parser (CDF file format)
[Mandatory] Impact Summary:
Denial of Service
[Optional] Trigger / Attack vector:
Malicious CDF file
[Mandatory] Key code/struct excerpt (minimal):
```c
			for (j = 0; j < nelements; j++, i++) {
				uint32_t l = CDF_GETUINT32(q, o);
				inp[i].pi_str.s_len = l;
				inp[i].pi_str.s_buf = (const char *)
				    (const void *)(&q[o4 + sizeof(l)]);
				DPRINTF(("l = %d, r = %d, s = %s\n", l,
				    CDF_ROUND(l, sizeof(l)),
				    inp[i].pi_str.s_buf));
				l = 4 + (uint32_t)CDF_ROUND(l, sizeof(l));
				o += l >> 2;
				if (q + o >= e)
					goto out;
				o4 = o * sizeof(uint32_t);
			}
```

[Mandatory] Trigger surface/attack vector:
File parser (CDF file format)

[Mandatory] Exploit primitive(s) available:
Out-of-bounds read

[Mandatory] Exploitability summary (1 sentence):
The vulnerability is easily triggered by processing a maliciously crafted CDF file, leading to an out-of-bounds read.

[Mandatory] Exploit script (summary, 3—6 bullets):
- Create a CDF file with a property section containing a CDF_LENGTH32_STRING or CDF_LENGTH32_WSTRING.
- Manipulate the length field of the string element to cause the offset calculation `o` to advance past the end of the section.
- The `q + o >= e` check is absent, so the loop reads past the buffer's end.
- Supply this file to an application using the vulnerable `file` library to parse CDF data.

Fix
[Mandatory] Fix code:
```c
			for (j = 0; j < nelements; j++, i++) {
				uint32_t l = CDF_GETUINT32(q, o);
				inp[i].pi_str.s_len = l;
				inp[i].pi_str.s_buf = (const char *)
				    (const void *)(&q[o4 + sizeof(l)]);
				DPRINTF(("l = %d, r = %d, s = %s\n", l,
				    CDF_ROUND(l, sizeof(l)),
				    inp[i].pi_str.s_buf));
				l = 4 + (uint32_t)CDF_ROUND(l, sizeof(l));
				o += l >> 2;
				if (q + o >= e)
					goto out;
				o4 = o * sizeof(uint32_t);
			}
```

[Mandatory] Fix summary:
The patch adds a bounds check `if (q + o >= e) goto out;` within the loop to ensure that the calculated pointer does not exceed the end of the buffer before it is used.

[Optional] Patch reference:
https://github.com/file/file/commit/1859fdb4e67c49c463c4e0078054335cd46ba295

What did the fix do?

cdf_read_sector buffer overflow

[Optional] Disclosure / Patch Dates:
Initial advisory: NA — Patch release: NA

The Vulnerability
[Optional] CWE/CVE Number and description:
CWE-119
[Mandatory] Summary:
The vulnerability exists in the `cdf_read_sector` function where an assertion `assert(ss == len)` is used to validate that the sector size matches the requested length. This check can be disabled in production builds, leading to a potential buffer overflow when `len` exceeds the actual sector size, allowing out-of-bounds writes via the `cdf_read` call.
[Mandatory] Root cause:
Reliance on a debug-only `assert` for bounds checking instead of runtime validation.
[Mandatory] Attack Surface:
File parser (CDF format)
[Mandatory] Impact Summary:
Out-of-bounds write → Potential code execution or denial of service
[Optional] Trigger / Attack vector:
Malformed CDF file
[Mandatory] Key code/struct excerpt (minimal):
```c
size_t ss = CDF_SEC_SIZE(h);
size_t pos = CDF_SEC_POS(h, id);
assert(ss == len);
return cdf_read(info, (off_t)pos, ((char *)buf) + offs, len);
```
Exploit:

[Mandatory] Trigger surface/attack vector:
File parsing (CDF format)

[Mandatory] Exploit primitive(s) available:
Out-of-bounds write

[Mandatory] Exploitability summary (1 sentence):
Exploitable if assertions are disabled, allowing controlled buffer overflow via crafted file input.

[Mandatory] Exploit script (summary, 3—6 bullets):
- Craft a CDF file with a sector where `len` does not match `CDF_SEC_SIZE(h)`.
- Ensure the file passes initial parsing to reach `cdf_read_sector`.
- Trigger the out-of-bounds write via the `cdf_read` call.
- Potentially corrupt memory to achieve code execution or crash.

Fix
[Mandatory] Fix code:
```c
size_t ss = CDF_SEC_SIZE(h);
size_t pos = CDF_SEC_POS(h, id);
if (ss != len) {
    // Handle error, e.g., return -1 or set errno
    return -1;
}
return cdf_read(info, (off_t)pos, ((char *)buf) + offs, len);
```

[Mandatory] Fix summary:
Replaced the `assert(ss == len)` with a runtime check to prevent buffer overflow when sector size does not match the requested length.

[Optional] Patch reference:
Commit 1859fdb4e67c49c463c4e0078054335cd46ba295
[Optional] Patch Analysis:
What did the fix do?

- Audit all file parsing code for missing bounds checks.

commit_message:
cred: copy_process() should clear child->replacement_session_keyring

keyctl_session_to_parent(task) sets ->replacement_session_keyring,
it should be processed and cleared by key_replace_session_keyring().

However, this task can fork before it notices TIF_NOTIFY_RESUME and
the new child gets the bogus ->replacement_session_keyring copied by
dup_task_struct(). This is obviously wrong and, if nothing else, this
leads to put_cred(already_freed_cred).

change copy_creds() to clear this member. If copy_process() fails
before this point the wrong ->replacement_session_keyring doesn't
matter, exit_creds() won't be called.

```c
        /* Copy actual data into new samples buffer */
        for (i = 0; samplesref->data[i]; i++)
            memcpy(link->cur_buf->data[i], samplesref->data[i], samplesref->linesize[0]);
```

commit_message:
refactor pyfribidi.c module

pyfribidi.c is now compiled as _pyfribidi. This module only handles
unicode internally and doesn't use the fribidi_utf8_to_unicode
function (which can't handle 4 byte utf-8 sequences). This fixes the
buffer overflow in issue #2.

The code is now also much simpler: pyfribidi.c is down from 280 to 130
lines of code.

We now ship a pure python pyfribidi that handles the case when
non-unicode strings are passed in.

We now also adapt the size of the output string if clean=True is
passed.

[Optional] CWE/CVE Number and description:

This can lead to an out-of-bounds read and write when processing specially crafted XML attributes, potentially causing memory corruption.

XML parser

[Optional] Trigger / Attack vector:
Malformed XML attribute value

    if ((in_space) && (normalize)) {
        while (buf[len - 1] == 0x20) len--;
    }
    buf[len] = 0;

Malformed XML attribute value
[Mandatory] Exploit primitive(s) available:
Out-of-bounds read/write

Exploitable by crafting an XML attribute that results in an empty buffer after normalization, leading to predictable memory corruption.

commit_message:
tjLoadImage: Fix issues w/loading 16-bit PPMs/PGMs

- The PPM reader now throws an error rather than segfaulting (due to a
  buffer overrun) if an application attempts to load a 16-bit PPM file
  into a grayscale uncompressed image buffer.  No known applications
  allowed that (not even the test applications in libjpeg-turbo),
  because that mode of operation was never expected to work and did not
  work under any circumstances.  (In fact, it was necessary to modify
  TJBench in order to reproduce the issue outside of a fuzzing
  environment.)  This was purely a matter of making the library bow out
  gracefully rather than crash if an application tries to do something
  really stupid.

- The PPM reader now throws an error rather than generating incorrect
  pixels if an application attempts to load a 16-bit PGM file into an
  RGB uncompressed image buffer.

- The PPM reader now correctly loads 16-bit PPM files into extended
  RGB uncompressed image buffers.  (Previously it generated incorrect
  pixels unless the input colorspace was JCS_RGB or JCS_EXT_RGB.)

The only way that users could have potentially encountered these issues
was through the tjLoadImage() function.  cjpeg and TJBench were
unaffected.

commit_message:
floppy: disable FDRAWCMD by default

Minh Yuan reported a concurrency use-after-free issue in the floppy code
between raw_cmd_ioctl and seek_interrupt.

[ It turns out this has been around, and that others have reported the
  KASAN splats over the years, but Minh Yuan had a reproducer for it and
  so gets primary credit for reporting it for this fix   - Linus ]

The problem is, this driver tends to break very easily and nowadays,
nobody is expected to use FDRAWCMD anyway since it was used to
manipulate non-standard formats.  The risk of breaking the driver is
higher than the risk presented by this race, and accessing the device
requires privileges anyway.

Let's just add a config option to completely disable this ioctl and
leave it disabled by default.  Distros shouldn't use it, and only those
running on antique hardware might need to enable it.

JavaScript code execution environment

```c
    capability = pargs->capability;

    array = args->data;

                            1, &next);
    if (njs_slow_path(ret == NJS_ERROR)) {
        return ret;
    }
```

JavaScript code executing Promise aggregation methods on crafted array-like objects.

commit_message:
Fixed aggregation methods of Promise ctor with array-like object.

Previously, while iterating over an array-like object the methods may be
resolved with INVALID values. INVALID value is a special internal type which
should never be visible by ordinary functions.

The fix is to ensure that absent elements are represented by undefined value.

The following methods were fixed Promise.all(), Promise.allSettled(),
    Promise.any(), Promise.race().

This closes #483 issue on Github.

case DUL_TYPETRANSFERSYNTAX:

The function assigns this unsigned length to a signed integer `nbytes`, which can lead to an incorrect comparison and an oversized `linebytes` value. This oversized value is then passed to an I2C read function with a fixed-size stack buffer (`linebuf`), causing a stack buffer overflow.

The root cause is a signed to unsigned integer conversion and comparison error where a large unsigned length value becomes a negative signed value, bypassing a size check.

Local command-line interface
[Mandatory] Impact Summary:
Local arbitrary code execution via stack buffer overflow

```c
	do {
		unsigned char	linebuf[DISP_LINE_LEN];
		unsigned char	*cp;

		linebytes = (nbytes > DISP_LINE_LEN) ? DISP_LINE_LEN : nbytes;

#if CONFIG_IS_ENABLED(DM_I2C)
		ret = dm_i2c_read(dev, addr, linebuf, linebytes);
#else
		ret = i2c_read(chip, addr, alen, linebuf, linebytes);
#endif
```

`i2c md` command line interface

- Attacker executes the `i2c md` command with a specific chip address, data address, and a large length (e.g., `i2c md 0 0 80000100`).
- The large length value causes `nbytes` to become negative, bypassing the `DISP_LINE_LEN` check.
- The `i2c_read` or `dm_i2c_read` function is called, attempting to write more than `DISP_LINE_LEN` bytes into the 16-byte `linebuf` stack buffer.

commit_message:
i2c: fix stack buffer overflow vulnerability in i2c md command

When running "i2c md 0 0 80000100", the function do_i2c_md parses the
length into an unsigned int variable named length. The value is then
moved to a signed variable:

    int nbytes = length;
    #define DISP_LINE_LEN 16
    int linebytes = (nbytes > DISP_LINE_LEN) ? DISP_LINE_LEN : nbytes;
    ret = dm_i2c_read(dev, addr, linebuf, linebytes);

On systems where integers are 32 bits wide, 0x80000100 is a negative
value to "nbytes > DISP_LINE_LEN" is false and linebytes gets assigned
0x80000100 instead of 16.

The consequence is that the function which reads from the i2c device
(dm_i2c_read or i2c_read) is called with a 16-byte stack buffer to fill
but with a size parameter which is too large. In some cases, this could
trigger a crash. But with some i2c drivers, such as drivers/i2c/nx_i2c.c
(used with "nexell,s5pxx18-i2c" bus), the size is actually truncated to
a 16-bit integer. This is because function i2c_transfer expects an
unsigned short length. In such a case, an attacker who can control the
response of an i2c device can overwrite the return address of a function
and execute arbitrary code through Return-Oriented Programming.

Fix this issue by using unsigned integers types in do_i2c_md. While at
it, make also alen unsigned, as signed sizes can cause vulnerabilities
when people forgot to check that they can be negative.

Signed-off-by: Nicolas Iooss <nicolas.iooss+uboot@ledger.fr>
Reviewed-by: Heiko Schocher <hs@denx.de>

[Optional] CWE/CVE Number and description:

[Mandatory] Summary:
 A vulnerability exists in the `get_alen` function within the U-Boot I2C command handler. The function parses an address length from an input string without validating that the character following a '.' is a digit. U-Boot command-line interface (CLI)

```c
		for (j = 0; j < 8; j++) {
			if (arg[j] == '.') {
				alen = arg[j+1] - '0';
				break;
			} else if (arg[j] == '\0')
				break;
		}
```

[Mandatory] Trigger surface/attack vector:
U-Boot CLI `i2c md` command
[Mandatory] Exploit primitive(s) available:
stack OOB write
[Mandatory] Exploitability summary (1 sentence):
Exploitable on systems with vulnerable I2C drivers where an attacker can control the device's response data, allowing for precise control over the data written past the stack buffer.
[Mandatory] Exploit script (summary, 3—6 bullets):
- Attacker gains access to the U-Boot command prompt.
- Attacker issues the `i2c md` command with a specially crafted length argument.
- This argument is parsed by `get_alen`, which can return a large length value if a non-digit follows a '.'.
- The large length value can bypass a subsequent check due to signed/unsigned mismatch in the calling function (`do_i2c_md`).
- An I2C read function is called with this large length and a small stack buffer as the destination.
- If the attacker controls the I2C device response, they can overflow the stack buffer and overwrite the return address to achieve RCE.

Fix
[Mandatory] Fix code:
```c
		for (j = 0; j < 8; j++) {
			if (arg[j] == '.') {
				if (arg[j+1] >= '0' && arg[j+1] <= '9') {
					alen = arg[j+1] - '0';
				}
				break;
			} else if (arg[j] == '\0')
				break;
		}
```

 The patch adds a bounds check to ensure that the character used to calculate the address length is a digit. This prevents an attacker from providing a non-numeric character that would result in an unexpectedly large length value.

The primary fix changed variable types from signed `int` to unsigned `uint` in the `do_i2c_md` function and `get_alen` to prevent a large unsigned value from being interpreted as a negative number, which bypassed a length check.

commit_message:
i2c: fix stack buffer overflow vulnerability in i2c md command

When running "i2c md 0 0 80000100", the function do_i2c_md parses the
length into an unsigned int variable named length. The value is then
moved to a signed variable:

    int nbytes = length;
    #define DISP_LINE_LEN 16
    int linebytes = (nbytes > DISP_LINE_LEN) ? DISP_LINE_LEN : nbytes;
    ret = dm_i2c_read(dev, addr, linebuf, linebytes);

On systems where integers are 32 bits wide, 0x80000100 is a negative
value to "nbytes > DISP_LINE_LEN" is false and linebytes gets assigned
0x80000100 instead of 16.

The consequence is that the function which reads from the i2c device
(dm_i2c_read or i2c_read) is called with a 16-byte stack buffer to fill
but with a size parameter which is too large. In some cases, this could
trigger a crash. But with some i2c drivers, such as drivers/i2c/nx_i2c.c
(used with "nexell,s5pxx18-i2c" bus), the size is actually truncated to
a 16-bit integer. This is because function i2c_transfer expects an
unsigned short length. In such a case, an attacker who can control the
response of an i2c device can overwrite the return address of a function
and execute arbitrary code through Return-Oriented Programming.

Fix this issue by using unsigned integers types in do_i2c_md. While at
it, make also alen unsigned, as signed sizes can cause vulnerabilities
when people forgot to check that they can be negative.

commit_message:
Save stack space while handling errors

Because error handling (luaG_errormsg) uses slots from EXTRA_STACK,
and some errors can recur (e.g., string overflow while creating an
error message in 'luaG_runerror', or a C-stack overflow before calling
the message handler), the code should use stack slots with parsimony.

This commit fixes the bug "Lua-stack overflow when C stack overflows
while handling an error".

Out-of-bounds write in cmdline window

[Optional] Affected products/versions:

The Vulnerability
[Optional] CWE/CVE Number and description:
CWE-787
[Mandatory] Summary:
The vulnerability occurs in the parse_command_modifiers function when handling the cmdline window in Ex mode. When processing a Visual mode range with an empty command, the code copies the string "'<,'>+" which can exceed the allocated memory buffer, leading to an out-of-bounds write. This happens specifically in the use_plus_cmd special case handling where mch_memmove and STRCPY operations write beyond the original command buffer allocation.
[Mandatory] Root cause:
Unchecked buffer length when copying Visual mode range string "'<,'>+" in Ex mode.
[Mandatory] Attack Surface:
Command line interface (Ex mode)
[Mandatory] Impact Summary:
Memory corruption → Potential code execution
[Optional] Trigger / Attack vector:
Ex mode command with Visual range and empty command
[Mandatory] Key code/struct excerpt (minimal):

```c
if (use_plus_cmd)
{
    size_t len = STRLEN(cmd_start);

    // Special case: empty command uses "+":
    //  "'<,'>mods" -> "mods'<,'>+"
    mch_memmove(orig_cmd, cmd_start, len);
    STRCPY(orig_cmd + len, "'<,'>+");
}
```

Exploit:

[Mandatory] Trigger surface/attack vector:
Ex mode command line with Visual range

[Mandatory] Exploit primitive(s) available:
Out-of-bounds write beyond allocated buffer

[Mandatory] Exploitability summary (1 sentence):
The vulnerability is triggered by entering Ex mode with a Visual range and empty command, allowing controlled out-of-bounds memory write.

[Mandatory] Exploit script (summary, 3—6 bullets):
- Enter Ex mode
- Use Visual mode range "'<,'>" 
- Enter an empty command after modifiers
- The buffer overflow occurs when processing the empty command
- Memory beyond allocated buffer is overwritten with "'<,'>+"

Fix
[Mandatory] Fix code:
```c
if (use_plus_cmd)
{
    size_t len = STRLEN(cmd_start);

    // Special case: empty command uses "+":
    //  "'<,'>mods" -> "mods *+"
    //  Use "*" instead of "'<,'>" to avoid the command getting
    //  longer, in case is was allocated.
    mch_memmove(orig_cmd, cmd_start, len);
    STRCPY(orig_cmd + len, " *+");
}
```

[Mandatory] Fix summary:
The patch replaces the 6-character string "'<,'>+" with the 3-character string " *+" to prevent buffer overflow when copying into the allocated command buffer.

commit_message:
XwdLoader: Fix buffer over-read and improve general robustness

This commit fixes a buffer over-read that could occur due to g_ntohl()
evaluating its argument more than once if at least one of the following
is true:

* Build target is not x86.
* __OPTIMIZE__ is not set during compilation (e.g. -O0 was used).

It also improves robustness more generally and fixes an issue where the
wrong field was being used to calculate the color map size, causing some
image files that were otherwise fine to be rejected.

Reported by @JieyongMa via huntr.dev.

net: rose: fix UAF bugs caused by timer handler

There are UAF bugs in rose_heartbeat_expiry(), rose_timer_expiry()
and rose_idletimer_expiry(). The root cause is that del_timer()
could not stop the timer handler that is running and the refcount
of sock is not managed properly.

  case ROSE_STATE_0     |
  rose_destroy_socket   |  rose_heartbeat_expiry
    rose_stop_heartbeat |
    sock_put(sk)        |    ...
  sock_put(sk) // FREE  |
                        |    bh_lock_sock(sk) // USE

[Mandatory] Title: CVE-2022-2318 / CWE-416:
net/rose: UAF in timer handler

[Optional] Disclosure / Patch Dates:
Initial advisory: 2022-07-06 — Patch release: 2022-06-28

[Optional] Affected products/versions:
Linux kernel from 2.6.12-rc2 to commit 9cc02ede696272c5271a401e4f27c262359bc2f6

The Vulnerability
[Optional] CWE/CVE Number and description:
 CWE-416: Use After Free
[Mandatory] Summary:
 A use-after-free vulnerability exists in the net/rose protocol subsystem due to a race condition between socket release and a timer handler. The rose_release() function can free a socket object while a timer handler like rose_heartbeat_expiry() is still executing, which then accesses the freed memory. This occurs because the original code used del_timer(), which does not prevent a running timer from accessing the socket after it has been freed.
[Mandatory] Root cause:
 The use of del_timer() does not guarantee that a running timer handler has stopped, leading to a use-after-free when the socket's reference count is not properly managed.
[Mandatory] Attack Surface:
Local user interacting with the Rose protocol network stack
[Mandatory] Impact Summary:
Kernel Denial of Service
[Optional] Trigger / Attack vector:
 Local user triggering a race condition between socket release and timer expiration
[Mandatory] Key code/struct excerpt (minimal):
del_timer(&rose_sk(sk)->timer);

Exploit:

[Mandatory] Trigger surface/attack vector:
Local interaction with the Rose protocol stack (e.g., creating, connecting, and releasing a socket)

[Mandatory] Exploit primitive(s) available:
Write to freed memory

[Mandatory] Exploitability summary (1 sentence):
Easily triggered by a local user with access to the Rose protocol, but exploitation to achieve code execution is difficult and depends on kernel memory management configurations.

[Mandatory] Exploit script (summary, 3—6 bullets):
- Create a Rose socket.
- Bind and connect the socket to start a heartbeat timer.
- Wait for the timer to be scheduled to run.
- Release the socket, which frees the socket object.
- The timer handler fires and attempts to use the now-freed socket, triggering the use-after-free and kernel panic.

Fix
[Mandatory] Fix code:
void rose_stop_timer(struct sock *sk)
{
	sk_stop_timer(sk, &rose_sk(sk)->timer);
}

[Mandatory] Fix summary:

The Vulnerability
[Optional] CWE/CVE Number and description:
CWE-416: Use After Free
[Mandatory] Summary:
A use-after-free vulnerability exists in the `rose_heartbeat_expiry` function in `net/rose/rose_timer.c`. The issue occurs due to a race condition between the socket release process in `rose_release` and the timer handler `rose_heartbeat_expiry`. If the socket is freed by `rose_release` while the timer handler is still executing, the handler will access the freed socket object via `bh_lock_sock(sk)`, leading to a use-after-free condition. This is exploitable because the timer can be triggered by an attacker, and the reference count on the socket object is not correctly managed, allowing it to be freed while still in use, as detailed in the commit message.
[Mandatory] Root cause:
The socket reference count is not properly decremented before the timer handler exits, allowing the socket to be freed while the timer handler is still running.
[Mandatory] Attack Surface:
ROSE protocol networking stack in the Linux kernel
[Mandatory] Impact Summary:
Denial of Service (kernel crash)
[Optional] Trigger / Attack vector:
Creating and then closing a ROSE socket while a heartbeat timer is active.
[Mandatory] Key code/struct excerpt (minimal):

static void rose_heartbeat_expiry(struct timer_list *t)
{
	struct sock *sk = from_timer(sk, t, sk_timer);
	struct rose_sock *rose = rose_sk(sk);
	bh_lock_sock(sk);
	// ...
	}

	rose_start_heartbeat(sk);
	bh_unlock_sock(sk);
	sock_put(sk);
}

Exploit:

[Mandatory] Trigger surface/attack vector:
ROSE protocol socket creation, connection, and closure operations.

[Mandatory] Exploit primitive(s) available:
Use-after-free (UAF) on a kernel socket object.

[Mandatory] Exploitability summary (1 sentence):
The race condition is locally triggerable with low complexity, providing a use-after-free primitive on a kernel object, which could lead to memory corruption or denial of service.

[Mandatory] Exploit script (summary, 3—6 bullets):
-   Create a ROSE socket using `socket()`.
-   Bind and connect the socket, which starts a heartbeat timer via `rose_start_heartbeat()`.
-   Close the socket from one thread, triggering `rose_release()` and `sock_put()`.
-   Simultaneously, the timer handler `rose_heartbeat_expiry()` executes in another context (interrupt/softirq) and accesses the now-freed socket object.
-   This access (e.g., `bh_lock_sock(sk)`) triggers the use-after-free bug.

Fix
[Mandatory] Fix code:
static void rose_heartbeat_expiry(struct timer_list *t)
{
	struct sock *sk = from_timer(sk, t, sk_timer);
	struct rose_sock *rose = rose_sk(sk);
	bh_lock_sock(sk);
	// ...
	}

	rose_start_heartbeat(sk);
	bh_unlock_sock(sk);
	sock_put(sk);
}

[Mandatory] Fix summary:
The patch adds two missing `sock_put(sk)` calls to properly decrement the socket's reference count. One is added before returning in the `ROSE_STATE_0` case, and another is added at the end of the function, ensuring the socket is not freed while the timer handler is still using it.

[Optional] Patch reference:
https://github.com/torvalds/linux/commit/9cc02ede696272c5271a401e4f27c262359bc2f6
[Optional] Patch Analysis:
What did the fix do?
- Field: PatchType (e.g., bounds check added, logic refactor, feature removal)
PatchType: Reference count management fix
[Optional] Variant & Triage Guidance

[Optional] Variant analysis suggestions (2—3 bullets):
-   Audit `rose_timer_expiry()` and `rose_idletimer_expiry()` for identical reference counting issues, as mentioned in the commit message.
-   Fuzz the ROSE protocol stack, focusing on race conditions between socket release and timer callbacks.
-   Review other kernel networking protocol implementations that use similar timer-and-socket patterns to ensure proper reference counting.

[Optional] Likely variants/impact (one line):
Similar use-after-free bugs likely exist in other timer handlers within the ROSE subsystem and potentially other kernel networking protocols.

The Vulnerability
[Optional] CWE/CVE Number and description:
CWE-416: Use After Free
[Mandatory] Summary:
A use-after-free (UAF) vulnerability was found in the ROSE protocol implementation. The bug occurs when a socket is freed by one thread while a timer, started by a function like `rose_start_hbtimer`, is still active and expires in another thread. The timer's callback then accesses the freed socket, leading to memory corruption because `del_timer()` does not stop a running timer and the socket's reference count is not properly managed.
[Mandatory] Root cause:
Timer management functions failed to handle running timers, leading to incorrect reference counting after socket deallocation.
[Mandatory] Attack Surface:
Linux kernel network stack (ROSE protocol)
[Mandatory] Impact Summary:
Kernel memory corruption → Denial of Service
[Optional] Trigger / Attack vector:
Local user with access to create and manipulate ROSE sockets triggering a race condition.
[Mandatory] Key code/struct excerpt (minimal):
```c
void rose_start_hbtimer(struct sock *sk)
{
	struct rose_sock *rose = rose_sk(sk);

	del_timer(&rose->timer);

	rose->timer.function = rose_timer_expiry;
	rose->timer.expires  = jiffies + rose->hb;

	add_timer(&rose->timer);
}
```
Exploit:

[Mandatory] Trigger surface/attack vector:
Local user with access to create and manipulate ROSE sockets.

[Mandatory] Exploit primitive(s) available:
Use-after-free leading to arbitrary read/write of freed socket memory.

[Mandatory] Exploitability summary (1 sentence):
Exploitable locally by a user who can create ROSE sockets, requiring a race condition between socket release and timer expiry.

[Mandatory] Exploit script (summary, 3—6 bullets):
- Create a ROSE socket and bind/connect it.
- Trigger a function that starts a heartbeat timer (e.g., `rose_start_hbtimer`).
- In a separate thread, close and release the socket.
- Wait for the timer to expire in the original context.
- The timer handler (`rose_heartbeat_expiry`) will access the freed socket, triggering the UAF.

Fix
[Mandatory] Fix code:
```c
void rose_start_hbtimer(struct sock *sk)
{
	struct rose_sock *rose = rose_sk(sk);

	sk_stop_timer(sk, &rose->timer);

	rose->timer.function = rose_timer_expiry;
	rose->timer.expires  = jiffies + rose->hb;

	sk_reset_timer(sk, &rose->timer, rose->timer.expires);
}
```

[Mandatory] Fix summary:
The patch replaces the unsafe `del_timer` and `add_timer` calls with `sk_stop_timer` and `sk_reset_timer`. These new functions correctly manage the socket's reference count during timer operations, preventing use-after-free.

https://github.com/torvalds/linux/commit/9cc02ede696272c5271a401e4f27c262359bc2f6

The Vulnerability
[Optional] CWE/CVE Number and description:
CWE-416: Use After Free
[Mandatory] Summary:
A use-after-free vulnerability exists in the Linux kernel's Rose protocol implementation. The flaw occurs in timer handlers like rose_timer_expiry because del_timer() does not prevent a handler that is already running from executing, and the socket's reference count is not correctly managed. This allows a timer to access and use a socket structure after it has been freed, as seen in the rose_start_t2timer function which sets up the timer.
[Mandatory] Root cause:
Incorrect use of del_timer() and improper socket reference count management.
[Mandatory] Attack Surface:
Kernel networking subsystem (Rose protocol)
[Mandatory] Impact Summary:
Local Denial of Service (kernel crash)
[Optional] Trigger / Attack vector:
Local access and execution of Rose protocol operations, triggering a race condition with timer expiry.
[Mandatory] Key code/struct excerpt (minimal):
void rose_start_t2timer(struct sock *sk)
{
	struct rose_sock *rose = rose_sk(sk);

	del_timer(&rose->timer);

	rose->timer.function = rose_timer_expiry;
	rose->timer.expires  = jiffies + rose->t2;

	add_timer(&rose->timer);
}
Exploit:

[Mandatory] Trigger surface/attack vector:
Local access to the Rose protocol, triggering a race condition during socket release and timer expiry.

[Mandatory] Exploit primitive(s) available:
Use-after-free leading to arbitrary write (spinlock)

[Mandatory] Exploitability summary (1 sentence):
The race condition is reliable to trigger with local access, leading to a kernel crash and potential memory corruption.

[Mandatory] Exploit script (summary, 3—6 bullets):
- Create and bind a Rose socket.
- Connect the socket, which starts a timer (e.g., via rose_start_t2timer).
- In a separate thread, trigger the socket's release (rose_release).
- Race the socket's deallocation (sock_put) with the execution of the already-running timer handler (rose_timer_expiry).
- The timer handler will then access the freed socket object, causing a use-after-free.

Fix
[Mandatory] Fix code:
void rose_start_t2timer(struct sock *sk)
{
	struct rose_sock *rose = rose_sk(sk);

	sk_stop_timer(sk, &rose->timer);

	rose->timer.function = rose_timer_expiry;
	rose->timer.expires  = jiffies + rose->t2;

	sk_reset_timer(sk, &rose->timer, rose->timer.expires);
}

[Mandatory] Fix summary:
The patch replaces del_timer() and add_timer() with sk_stop_timer() and sk_reset_timer(). These new functions correctly manage the socket's reference count, ensuring the socket is not freed while a timer handler might still be executing.
[Optional] Patch reference:
https://github.com/torvalds/linux/commit/9cc02ede696272c5271a401e4f27c262359bc2f6
[Optional] Patch Analysis:
Short note: "What did the fix do?"
- Field: PatchType (e.g., bounds check added, logic refactor, feature removal)
logic refactor
[Optional] Variant & Triage Guidance

[Optional] Variant analysis suggestions (2—3 bullets):
- Review other network protocol implementations in the kernel for similar timer refcounting issues.
- Audit all uses of del_timer() and add_timer() to ensure they are not used on objects that can be freed from another context without proper synchronization or refcounting.
- Fuzz the Rose protocol and other similar subsystems with a focus on concurrent socket operations and timer expirations.

[Optional] Likely variants/impact (one line):
Similar timer-based UAF bugs are likely in other kernel subsystems with asynchronous object lifecycles.

The Vulnerability
[Optional] CWE/CVE Number and description:
CWE-416: Use After Free
[Mandatory] Summary:
A use-after-free vulnerability exists in the net/rose subsystem due to a race condition between socket release (`rose_release`) and timer handler functions (`rose_timer_expiry`, etc.). The socket can be freed while a timer is still active, allowing the timer handler to access the freed memory later. This occurs because `del_timer()` does not prevent an already-running handler from executing, and the socket's reference count is not held by the timer logic.
[Mandatory] Root cause:
The timer handler uses a socket after it has been freed because `del_timer()` does not stop a running handler and the socket reference count is not held by the timer.
[Mandatory] Attack Surface:
Local kernel network interface (rose protocol)
[Mandatory] Impact Summary:
Local Denial of Service (kernel crash)
[Optional] Trigger / Attack vector:
Local user creating and closing a rose socket to trigger the race condition.
[Mandatory] Key code/struct excerpt (minimal):
void rose_start_t1timer(struct sock *sk)
{
	struct rose_sock *rose = rose_sk(sk);

	del_timer(&rose->timer);

	rose->timer.function = rose_timer_expiry;
	rose->timer.expires  = jiffies + rose->t1;

	add_timer(&rose->timer);
}
Exploit:

[Mandatory] Trigger surface/attack vector:
Local rose socket operations (create, connect, release)

[Mandatory] Exploit primitive(s) available:
Kernel memory corruption (use-after-free write)

[Mandatory] Exploitability summary (1 sentence):
The race condition is reliably triggerable by a local user, leading to a kernel crash and denial of service.

[Mandatory] Exploit script (summary, 3—6 bullets):
- Create a rose socket.
- Initiate a connection (`rose_connect`) to start a timer (e.g., `rose_start_heartbeat`).
- In a separate thread, close the socket (`rose_release`), which frees the socket structure.
- Wait for the previously started timer to expire.
- The timer handler (`rose_heartbeat_expiry`) executes, accessing the now-freed socket, causing a use-after-free and kernel panic.

Fix
[Mandatory] Fix code:
void rose_start_t1timer(struct sock *sk)
{
	struct rose_sock *rose = rose_sk(sk);

	sk_stop_timer(sk, &rose->timer);

	rose->timer.function = rose_timer_expiry;
	rose->timer.expires  = jiffies + rose->t1;

	sk_reset_timer(sk, &rose->timer, rose->timer.expires);
}

[Mandatory] Fix summary:
The patch replaces the unsafe `del_timer()` and `add_timer()` calls with `sk_stop_timer()` and `sk_reset_timer()`, which properly manage the socket's reference count to prevent use-after-free during timer operations.
[Optional] Patch reference:
https://github.com/torvalds/linux/commit/9cc02ede696272c5271a401e4f27c262359bc2f6
[Optional] Patch Analysis:
What did the fix do?
- Field: PatchType (e.g., bounds check added, logic refactor, feature removal)
API change to add refcounting
[Optional] Variant & Triage Guidance

[Optional] Variant analysis suggestions (2—3 bullets):
- Review other timer start functions in the `net/rose` module (e.g., `rose_start_heartbeat`, `rose_start_idletimer`) for the same `del_timer`/`add_timer` pattern.
- Audit the corresponding timer expiry functions (`rose_heartbeat_expiry`, `rose_timer_expiry`, `rose_idletimer_expiry`) for proper socket handling.
- Fuzz the `net/rose` subsystem with concurrent socket creation/release operations to discover similar race conditions.

[Optional] Likely variants/impact (one line):
The same UAF pattern likely exists in the heartbeat and idletimer handlers.

void rose_start_idletimer(struct sock *sk)
{
	struct rose_sock *rose = rose_sk(sk);

	del_timer(&rose->idletimer);

	if (rose->idle > 0) {
		rose->idletimer.function = rose_idletimer_expiry;
		rose->idletimer.expires  = jiffies + rose->idle;

		add_timer(&rose->idletimer);

[Optional] CWE/CVE Number and description:
CWE-416: Use After Free
[Mandatory] Summary:
A use-after-free vulnerability exists in the Linux kernel's net/rose protocol handler. The bug is triggered when a socket is closed and freed via `rose_release()` while its heartbeat timer, started by `rose_start_heartbeat()`, is still active. The timer callback function `rose_heartbeat_expiry` then accesses the already-freed socket object, leading to a use-after-free condition that can be exploited for local privilege escalation or denial of service.
[Mandatory] Root cause:
The timer handler uses `del_timer()` and `add_timer()` which do not properly manage the socket's reference count, allowing the socket to be freed while the timer is still active.
[Mandatory] Attack Surface:
Kernel networking subsystem (ROSE protocol)
[Mandatory] Impact Summary:
Local privilege escalation / Denial of Service
[Optional] Trigger / Attack vector:
Local user with ability to create and close ROSE sockets
[Mandatory] Key code/struct excerpt (minimal):
```c
void rose_start_heartbeat(struct sock *sk)
{
	sk_stop_timer(sk, &sk->sk_timer);

	sk->sk_timer.function = rose_heartbeat_expiry;
	sk->sk_timer.expires  = jiffies + 5 * HZ;

	sk_reset_timer(sk, &sk->sk_timer, sk->sk_timer.expires);
}
```
Exploit:

[Mandatory] Trigger surface/attack vector:
Local socket operations (socket(), bind(), connect(), close()) on the ROSE protocol family

[Mandatory] Exploit primitive(s) available:
Use-after-free leading to arbitrary memory write on the freed socket object

Exploitable locally by a user who can create and manipulate ROSE sockets, as demonstrated by the provided proof-of-concept.

- Create a ROSE socket and initiate a connection.
- Start the heartbeat timer for the socket using `rose_start_heartbeat()`.
- In a separate thread, close and release the socket, which frees the socket object.
- The previously started timer handler `rose_heartbeat_expiry` executes.
- The handler attempts to lock the freed socket structure with `bh_lock_sock()`, triggering a use-after-free.

[Mandatory] Fix code:

```c
{
	sk_stop_timer(sk, &sk->sk_timer);

	sk->sk_timer.function = rose_heartbeat_expiry;
	sk->sk_timer.expires  = jiffies + 5 * HZ;

	sk_reset_timer(sk, &sk->sk_timer, sk->sk_timer.expires);
}
```

The patch replaces the unsafe `del_timer()` and `add_timer()` calls with `sk_stop_timer()` and `sk_reset_timer()`. These new functions properly manage the socket's reference count, ensuring the socket is not freed while its timer is active.

net: rose: fix UAF bugs caused by timer handler

There are UAF bugs in rose_heartbeat_expiry(), rose_timer_expiry()
and rose_idletimer_expiry(). The root cause is that del_timer()
could not stop the timer handler that is running and the refcount
of sock is not managed properly.

One of the UAF bugs is shown below:

    (thread 1)          |        (thread 2)
                        |  rose_bind
                        |  rose_connect
                        |    rose_start_heartbeat
rose_release            |    (wait a time)
  case ROSE_STATE_0     |
  rose_destroy_socket   |  rose_heartbeat_expiry
    rose_stop_heartbeat |
    sock_put(sk)        |    ...
  sock_put(sk) // FREE  |
                        |    bh_lock_sock(sk) // USE

The sock is deallocated by sock_put() in rose_release() and
then used by bh_lock_sock() in rose_heartbeat_expiry().

[Optional] CWE/CVE Number and description:

[Mandatory] Summary:
 A use-after-free vulnerability exists in the `regtilde` function within `src/regexp.c`. When processing a recursive substitute, the function could assign the `reg_prev_sub` pointer to a string (`newsub`) that might be freed in a subsequent call. This allows an attacker to trigger a use-after-free condition by crafting a specific regular expression substitution pattern.

Vim editor's regular expression substitution command

```c
    vim_free(reg_prev_sub);
    if (newsub != source)	// newsub was allocated, just keep it
	reg_prev_sub = newsub;
    else			// no ~ found, need to save newsub
	reg_prev_sub = vim_strsave(newsub);
```

Vim's regular expression substitution command (`:s`)

[Mandatory] Exploit primitive(s) available:
Use-after-free leading to potential arbitrary read/write.

[Optional] Disclosure / Patch Dates:

[Optional] Affected products/versions:
cJSON library versions prior to commit 94df772485c92866ca417d92137747b2e3b0a917

The Vulnerability
[Optional] CWE/CVE Number and description:
 Out-of-bounds read
[Mandatory] Summary:
 A vulnerability exists in the `parse_string` function within `cJSON.c`. When parsing a JSON string that ends with a backslash, the length calculation loop reads past the input's null terminator, causing an out-of-bounds read. This occurs because the original code `if (*end_ptr++ == '\\') end_ptr++;` does not check if the character following the backslash is the null terminator before incrementing the pointer.
[Mandatory] Root cause:
 Failure to check for a null terminator after a backslash during string length calculation.
[Mandatory] Attack Surface:
Any application using cJSON to parse untrusted JSON data
[Mandatory] Impact Summary:
Information disclosure via out-of-bounds read.
[Optional] Trigger / Attack vector:
 A specially crafted JSON string ending in a backslash character.
[Mandatory] Key code/struct excerpt (minimal):
if (*str!='\"') {*ep=str;return 0;} /* not a string! */

while (*end_ptr!='\"' && *end_ptr && ++len) if (*end_ptr++ == '\\') end_ptr++; /* Skip escaped quotes. */

out=(char*)cJSON_malloc(len+1); /* This is how long we need for the string, roughly. */
Exploit:

[Mandatory] Trigger surface/attack vector:
JSON parsing API (e.g., cJSON_Parse)

[Mandatory] Exploit primitive(s) available:
out-of-bounds read

[Mandatory] Exploitability summary (1 sentence):
Exploitability is high for any application processing untrusted JSON, as it requires only a single malformed string to trigger the read.

[Mandatory] Exploit script (summary, 3—6 bullets):
- Create a JSON string with a key and a string value.
- Ensure the string value ends with a single backslash (`\`).
- Feed this JSON string to an application using the vulnerable cJSON library.
- The application will call `parse_string`, triggering the out-of-bounds read.

Fix
[Mandatory] Fix code:
while (*end_ptr!='\"' && *end_ptr && ++len)
{
    if (*end_ptr++ == '\\')
    {
        if (*end_ptr == '\0')
        {
            /* prevent buffer overflow when last input character is a backslash */
            return 0;
        }
        end_ptr++; /* Skip escaped quotes. */
    }
}

[Mandatory] Fix summary:
 The patch adds a check to ensure that if a backslash is encountered, it is not the last character of the string (i.e., not followed by a null terminator) before advancing the pointer, preventing the out-of-bounds read.

The Vulnerability
[Optional] CWE/CVE Number and description:
CWE-787: Out-of-bounds Write
[Mandatory] Summary:
A vulnerability exists in the `findEndOfLine` function of `wangle/codec/LineBasedFrameDecoder.cpp`. The bug is triggered when the decoder processes a carriage return (`\r`) character that is not followed by a newline (`\n`). In this scenario, the code calls `c.read<char>()` to check for the subsequent newline without first verifying that the buffer has remaining bytes, resulting in an out-of-bounds read.
[Mandatory] Root cause:
An out-of-bounds read occurs due to a missing bounds check before calling `c.read<char>()` to inspect the next byte in the buffer.
[Mandatory] Attack Surface:
Network library
[Mandatory] Impact Summary:
Information disclosure
[Optional] Trigger / Attack vector:
Malicious network data stream
[Mandatory] Key code/struct excerpt (minimal):
```cpp
  auto b = c.read<char>();
  if (b == '\n' && terminatorType_ != TerminatorType::CARRIAGENEWLINE) {
    return i;
  } else if (terminatorType_ != TerminatorType::NEWLINE &&
             b == '\r' && !c.isAtEnd() && c.read<char>() == '\n') {
    return i;
  }
```
Exploit:

[Mandatory] Trigger surface/attack vector:
Network data parsing function

[Mandatory] Exploit primitive(s) available:
Out-of-bounds read

[Mandatory] Exploitability summary (1 sentence):
An attacker can trigger the out-of-bounds read by sending a crafted data stream ending in a lone '\r', allowing them to read one byte past the buffer's intended boundary.

[Mandatory] Exploit script (summary, 3—6 bullets):
- Establish a connection to a service utilizing the vulnerable Wangle library.
- Send a data payload that ends with a carriage return (`\r`) character.
- Ensure no newline (`\n`) character follows the carriage return.
- This causes the `findEndOfLine` function to call `c.read<char>()` when the buffer cursor is at the end, triggering the out-of-bounds read.
- The attacker can potentially read adjacent memory contents.

Fix
[Mandatory] Fix code:
```cpp
  } else if (
      terminatorType_ != TerminatorType::NEWLINE && b == '\r' &&
      !c.isAtEnd() && *c.peekBytes().data() == '\n') {
    return i;
  }
```
[Mandatory] Fix summary:
The patch replaces the `c.read<char>()` call with `*c.peekBytes().data()` for the newline check. This change ensures the function only inspects the next byte without advancing the buffer cursor, preventing the out-of-bounds read underflow condition.

https://github.com/facebook/wangle/commit/5b3bceca875e4ea4ed9d14c20b20ce46c92c13c6

What did the fix do?

- Fuzz the `LineBasedFrameDecoder` with various edge case inputs, including different terminator sequences and buffer boundary conditions.
- Audit other frame decoders or parsers in the Wangle library for similar cursor management issues.

[Optional] Likely variants/impact (one line):
Other parsers in the library using `Cursor::read` may have similar out-of-bounds read vulnerabilities.

commit_message:
Fixed arrays expansion.

There were two problems with njs_array_expand():

 1. It checked that the requred size with the appended elements wasn't bigger
    then the array size and then did nothing.  If there were elements removed
    from the beggining (by shift() operation), then "size <= array->size" can
    be true even if there wasn't enought free space after the array.

 2. After allocating more space to prepend elements, it set array->size without
    counting those elements.

Probably, the original idea was to decrement array->size while removing
elements from the beginning, but it wasn't done right.  Even if so, the
new version of the function looks cleaner.

This closes #152 and closes #153 issues on Github.

```c
{

	char s1[32]="", s2[32]="";
	sscanf(str + 4, "%d%[%%, \t]%d%[%%, \t]%d", &r, s1, &g, s2, &b);
	if (strchr(s1, '%')) {
		return NSVG_RGB((r*255)/100,(g*255)/100,(b*255)/100);
	} else {
		return NSVG_RGB(r,g,b);
	}
}
```

SVG file parsing

[Mandatory] Fix code:
```c
static unsigned int nsvg__parseColorRGB(const char* str)
{
	unsigned int r=0, g=0, b=0;
	if (sscanf(str, "rgb(%u, %u, %u)", &r, &g, &b) == 3)		// decimal integers
		return NSVG_RGB(r, g, b);
	if (sscanf(str, "rgb(%u%%, %u%%, %u%%)", &r, &g, &b) == 3)	// decimal integer percentage
		return NSVG_RGB(r*255/100, g*255/100, b*255/100);
	return NSVG_RGB(128, 128, 128);
}
```

commit_message:
device_tree.c: Don't use load_image()

The load_image() function is deprecated, as it does not let the
caller specify how large the buffer to read the file into is.
Instead use load_image_size().

The vulnerability exists in the read_and_process_frames function in audio_hw.c where proc_buf_out buffer is not consistently initialized when channel remapping is needed. This can lead to using uninitialized memory for audio processing, potentially causing memory corruption when frames are written to or read from this buffer.
[Mandatory] Root cause:
Inconsistent initialization of intermediate scratch buffers (proc_buf_out) when channel remapping is required.
[Mandatory] Attack Surface:
Audio processing subsystem
[Mandatory] Impact Summary:
Memory corruption → Potential code execution
[Optional] Trigger / Attack vector:
Audio recording with preprocessing enabled and channel remapping required
[Mandatory] Key code/struct excerpt (minimal):

```c
if (channel_remapping_needed) {
    /* With additional channels, we cannot use original buffer */
    if (in->proc_buf_size < src_buffer_size) {
        in->proc_buf_size = src_buffer_size;
        in->proc_buf_out = realloc(in->proc_buf_out, src_buffer_size);
        ALOG_ASSERT((in->proc_buf_out != NULL),
                    "process_frames() failed to reallocate proc_buf_out");
    }
    proc_buf_out = in->proc_buf_out;
}
```

Exploit:

[Mandatory] Trigger surface/attack vector:
Audio recording API with preprocessing effects

[Mandatory] Exploit primitive(s) available:
Out-of-bounds read/write, use of uninitialized memory

[Mandatory] Exploitability summary (1 sentence):
Exploitable through audio recording with specific channel configurations that trigger remapping.

[Mandatory] Exploit script (summary, 3—6 bullets):
- Initiate audio recording with preprocessing enabled
- Configure audio stream with mismatched channel counts requiring remapping
- Trigger frame processing to hit uninitialized buffer path
- Memory corruption occurs during adjust_channels operation
- Potential for controlled memory write/overwrite

Fix
[Mandatory] Fix code:
```c
/* With additional channels or processing, we need intermediate buffers */
if (channel_remapping_needed || has_processing) {
    const size_t src_buffer_size = frames_num * src_frame_size;

    if (in->proc_buf_size < src_buffer_size) {
        in->proc_buf_size = src_buffer_size;
#ifdef PREPROCESSING_ENABLED
        /* we always reallocate both buffers in case # of effects change dynamically. */
        in->proc_buf_in = realloc(in->proc_buf_in, src_buffer_size);
        ALOG_ASSERT((in->proc_buf_in != NULL),
                "process_frames() failed to reallocate proc_buf_in");
#endif
        in->proc_buf_out = realloc(in->proc_buf_out, src_buffer_size);
        ALOG_ASSERT((in->proc_buf_out != NULL),
                "process_frames() failed to reallocate proc_buf_out");
    }
    if (channel_remapping_needed) {
        proc_buf_out = in->proc_buf_out;
    }
}
```

[Mandatory] Fix summary:
The fix ensures proc_buf_out is consistently initialized for both channel remapping and preprocessing scenarios, and adds a check to prevent memory overwrite when frames_wr is negative.

The Vulnerability
[Optional] CWE/CVE Number and description:
 Out-of-bounds Read
[Mandatory] Summary:
 The bug exists in the `bfd_get_debug_link_info_1` function in `bfd/opncls.c`. It is triggered when processing a specially crafted `.gnu_debuglink` section where the calculated offset for the CRC value is at the end of the section. An incorrect bounds check (`>=` instead of `+ 4 >`) allows a 4-byte read past the end of the allocated buffer, leading to a potential crash or information leak.
[Mandatory] Root cause:
 Incorrect bounds check (`crc_offset >= bfd_get_section_size(sect)`) before a 4-byte read operation for the CRC value.
[Mandatory] Attack Surface:
Tools processing binary files (e.g., objdump, gdb) using the BFD library.
[Mandatory] Impact Summary:
Application Crash (Denial of Service)
[Optional] Trigger / Attack vector:
 A specially crafted binary file with a malicious .gnu_debuglink section.
[Mandatory] Key code/struct excerpt (minimal):
  /* PR 17597: avoid reading off the end of the buffer.  */
  crc_offset = strnlen (name, bfd_get_section_size (sect)) + 1;
  crc_offset = (crc_offset + 3) & ~3;
  if (crc_offset >= bfd_get_section_size (sect))
    return NULL;

  *crc32 = bfd_get_32 (abfd, contents + crc_offset);
  return name;

Exploit:

[Mandatory] Trigger surface/attack vector:
Specially crafted binary file with a malicious .gnu_debuglink section.

[Mandatory] Exploit primitive(s) available:
Out-of-bounds read (potential information leak or crash).

Easily triggered by processing a malicious file, leading to a potential crash.

[Mandatory] Exploit script (summary, 3—6 bullets):
- Create a binary file with a `.gnu_debuglink` section.
- Craft the section contents so that the filename length, when aligned up to a 4-byte boundary, places the `crc_offset` at the very end of the section.
- Ensure that `crc_offset + 4` exceeds the total size of the section.
- Open the crafted file with a tool (e.g., objdump) that uses the vulnerable BFD library.
- The tool will execute `bfd_get_32` at an out-of-bounds address, likely resulting in a segmentation fault.

Fix
[Mandatory] Fix code:
  /* PR 17597: avoid reading off the end of the buffer.  */
  crc_offset = strnlen (name, bfd_get_section_size (sect)) + 1;
  crc_offset = (crc_offset + 3) & ~3;
  if (crc_offset + 4 > bfd_get_section_size (sect))
    return NULL;

  *crc32 = bfd_get_32 (abfd, contents + crc_offset);

[Mandatory] Fix summary:
 The bounds check before reading the 4-byte CRC value was corrected from `crc_offset >= bfd_get_section_size (sect)` to `crc_offset + 4 > bfd_get_section_size (sect)` to ensure the read does not exceed the section's size.

 A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the `sanitize_proprietary_tags` function in `lib/ofx_preproc.cpp`. The function iterates over an input string without checking its length against the fixed-size stack buffer `tagname`. An attacker can provide a long string containing a tag, causing a stack-based buffer overflow when the tag name exceeds `READ_BUFFER_SIZE`, as shown in the key code excerpt where the loop iterates based on `input_string_size` but writes to the fixed-size `tagname` buffer.
[Mandatory] Root cause:
 The loop condition `i < input_string_size` does not prevent writes past the bounds of the fixed-size `tagname` buffer.

OFX file parser in libofx library
[Mandatory] Impact Summary:
Arbitrary Code Execution

 Specially crafted OFX file with a long proprietary tag name.
[Mandatory] Key code/struct excerpt (minimal):

```cpp
size_t input_string_size = input_string.size();

// Minimum workaround to prevent buffer overflow: Stop iterating
// once the (fixed!) size of the output buffers is reached.
for (i = 0; i < std::min(input_string_size, size_t(READ_BUFFER_SIZE)); i++)
{
  if (input_string.c_str()[i] == '<')
  {
    tag_open = true;
    tag_open_idx = i;
  }
  else if (tag_open == true && closing_tag_open == false)
  {
    tagname[tagname_idx] = input_string.c_str()[i];
    tagname_idx++;
  }
}
```
Exploit:

[Mandatory] Trigger surface/attack vector:
OFX file parser

[Mandatory] Exploit primitive(s) available:
Stack buffer overflow (write out of bounds)

[Mandatory] Exploitability summary (1 sentence):
The vulnerability allows an attacker to corrupt the stack by providing a long tag name in a crafted OFX file, potentially leading to code execution.

[Mandatory] Exploit script (summary, 3—6 bullets):
- Create a malicious OFX file.
- Include a proprietary tag with a name longer than `READ_BUFFER_SIZE`.
- The tag name should contain characters to be copied into the `tagname` buffer.
- When `libofx` parses the file, the `sanitize_proprietary_tags` function is called.
- The loop over the tag name will write past the `tagname` buffer on the stack.
- This corrupts stack memory, which can be leveraged for arbitrary code execution.

Fix
[Mandatory] Fix code:
```cpp
// Vulnerable:
// for (i = 0; i < input_string_size; i++)
//
// Fixed:
for (i = 0; i < std::min(input_string_size, size_t(READ_BUFFER_SIZE)); i++)
```

 The patch modified the main loop condition in `sanitize_proprietary_tags` to `std::min(input_string_size, size_t(READ_BUFFER_SIZE))`, preventing the loop index from exceeding the size of the fixed-size stack buffers.

commit_message:
Fix a buffer overflow.

This is only the minimum workaround to prevent buffer overflow:
Stop iterating once the (fixed!) size of the output buffers is
reached. In response to
https://www.talosintelligence.com/vulnerability_reports/TALOS-2017-0317

However, this code is a huge mess anyway and is in no way
anything like up-to-date C++ code. Please, anyone, replace it
with something more modern. Thanks.

Fix buffer overflows occurring reading redis.conf.

There was not enough sanity checking in the code loading the slots of
Redis Cluster from the nodes.conf file, this resulted into the
attacker's ability to write data at random addresses in the process
memory, by manipulating the index of the array. The bug seems
exploitable using the following techique: the config file may be altered so
that one of the nodes gets, as node ID (which is the first field inside the
structure) some data that is actually executable: then by writing this
address in selected places, this node ID part can be executed after a
jump. So it is mostly just a matter of effort in order to exploit the
bug. In practice however the issue is not very critical because the
bug requires an unprivileged user to be able to modify the Redis cluster
nodes configuration, and at the same time this should result in some
gain. However Redis normally is unprivileged as well. Yet much better to
have this fixed indeed.

Fix #4278.

The Vulnerability
[Optional] CWE/CVE Number and description:
CWE-119: Improper Restriction of Operations within the Bounds of a Memory Buffer
[Mandatory] Summary:
A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the `XkbVModIndexText` function within `xkb/xkbtext.c`. The function calculates the length of a string to be copied and requests a buffer of that size, but a prior bounds check on this length was removed. This allows an attacker to trigger a buffer overflow by providing input that results in a string longer than the fixed-size buffer returned by `tbGetBuffer`, leading to memory corruption.
[Mandatory] Root cause:
Removal of a bounds check on the calculated string length before copying it into a fixed-size buffer.
[Mandatory] Attack Surface:
Local X client or user with access to XKB configuration
[Mandatory] Impact Summary:
Local code execution via memory corruption
[Optional] Trigger / Attack vector:
Malicious XKB protocol request or configuration file
[Mandatory] Key code/struct excerpt (minimal):

len = strlen(tmp) + 1;
if (format == XkbCFile)
    len += 4;
rtrn = tbGetBuffer(len);
if (format == XkbCFile) {
    strcpy(rtrn, "vmod_");
    strncpy(&rtrn[5], tmp, len - 4);
}
else
    strncpy(rtrn, tmp, len);

Exploit:

[Mandatory] Trigger surface/attack vector:
Malicious XKB protocol request or configuration file

[Mandatory] Exploit primitive(s) available:
Stack/heap buffer overflow (potentially arbitrary write)

[Mandatory] Exploitability summary (1 sentence):
Exploitable by a local user who can influence XKB virtual modifier names to trigger a buffer overflow, potentially bypassing modern mitigations depending on the memory layout of the static buffer.

[Mandatory] Exploit script (summary, 3—6 bullets):
- Attacker gains local access to a system running the vulnerable Xorg server.
- Attacker identifies a method to set a very long name for a virtual modifier, possibly via a client-side application or by influencing configuration files.
- The attacker triggers the vulnerable code path, causing `XkbVModIndexText` to be called with an `ndx` corresponding to the long name.
- The function calculates a large `len`, requests a buffer, and copies the long string, overflowing the static buffer.
- The overflow corrupts adjacent memory, potentially overwriting function pointers or other control-flow data to achieve code execution.

Fix
[Mandatory] Fix code:
len = strlen(tmp) + 1;
if (format == XkbCFile)
    len += 4;
rtrn = tbGetBuffer(len);
if (format == XkbCFile) {
    strcpy(rtrn, "vmod_");
    strncpy(&rtrn[5], tmp, len - 4);
}
else
    strncpy(rtrn, tmp, len);

[Mandatory] Fix summary:
The patch replaced the fixed-size static buffer with a ring of resizable buffers via `tbGetBuffer`. Consequently, the length clamping check that was previously required to prevent overflows was removed.
[Optional] Patch reference:
https://cgit.freedesktop.org/xorg/xserver/commit/?id=94f11ca5cf011ef123bd222cabeaef6f424d76ac

What did the fix do?

- Review other functions in the XKB codebase that use `tbGetBuffer` or similar static buffers for string generation, as they may have similar issues.
- Fuzz the XKB protocol parser and configuration file parser with long strings to identify other potential overflows.
- Audit other parts of the Xorg server that rely on shared static buffers for dynamic content.

[Optional] Likely variants/impact (one line):
Other functions using the same static buffer mechanism are likely to have similar buffer overflow vulnerabilities.
commit_message:
Generating strings for XKB data used a single shared static buffer,
which offered several opportunities for errors. Use a ring of
resizable buffers instead, to avoid problems when strings end up
longer than anticipated.

The Vulnerability
[Optional] CWE/CVE Number and description:
CWE-125: Out-of-bounds Read
[Mandatory] Summary:
A vulnerability exists in the pcfGetProperties function within src/bitmap/pcfread.c. When processing a specially crafted PCF font file, the function can read past the end of an allocated buffer named 'strings' due to a lack of bounds checking. This allows an attacker to read arbitrary memory contents, potentially leading to information disclosure or a crash.
[Mandatory] Root cause:
The code uses strlen() on a pointer derived from an unchecked offset into the 'strings' buffer, leading to an out-of-bounds read.
[Mandatory] Attack Surface:
Font parsing library (libXfont)
[Mandatory] Impact Summary:
Local information disclosure and denial of service
[Optional] Trigger / Attack vector:
Malformed PCF font file
[Mandatory] Key code/struct excerpt (minimal):

for (i = 0; i < nprops; i++) {
	props[i].name = MakeAtom(strings + props[i].name,
				strlen(strings + props[i].name), TRUE);
	if (isStringProp[i]) {
	    props[i].value = MakeAtom(strings + props[i].value,
			      strlen(strings + props[i].value), TRUE);
	}
}
Exploit:

[Mandatory] Trigger surface/attack vector:
Font file parsing

[Mandatory] Exploit primitive(s) available:
Arbitrary memory read (relative to strings buffer)

[Mandatory] Exploitability summary (1 sentence):
Exploitable by a local attacker who can supply a malicious PCF file to an application using the vulnerable library.

[Mandatory] Exploit script (summary, 3—6 bullets):
- Create a malicious PCF file.
- Craft the `properties` section to include a string with a large offset value for a property name or value.
- Ensure this offset points outside the actual `strings` data buffer but within readable memory.
- Trigger the vulnerability by loading the font with a vulnerable application (e.g., X server).
- The application reads out-of-bounds via `strlen()` and potentially leaks the data through the atom table or crashes.

Fix
[Mandatory] Fix code:
for (i = 0; i < nprops; i++) {
	if (props[i].name >= string_size) {
	    pcfError("pcfGetProperties(): String starts out of bounds (%ld/%d)\n", props[i].name, string_size);
	    goto Bail;
	}
	props[i].name = MakeAtom(strings + props[i].name,
				strnlen(strings + props[i].name, string_size - props[i].name), TRUE);
	if (isStringProp[i]) {
	    if (props[i].value >= string_size) {
		pcfError("pcfGetProperties(): String starts out of bounds (%ld/%d)\n", props[i].value, string_size);
		goto Bail;
	    }
	    props[i].value = MakeAtom(strings + props[i].value,
			      strnlen(strings + props[i].value, string_size - props[i].value), TRUE);
	}
}

[Mandatory] Fix summary:
The patch adds bounds checks to ensure that property name and value offsets are within the allocated 'strings' buffer. It also replaces the unsafe strlen() calls with strnlen() to prevent reading past the buffer's end.

commit_message:
Bug 698592: Mark variable fz_var(), avoiding optimization.

The change in 2707fa9e8e6d17d794330e719dec1b08161fb045
in build_filter_chain() allows for the variable chain
to reside in a register, which means that the bug is
likely to only be visible if built under optimization.

First the chain variable is transferred to chain2, then
set to NULL, then when an exception occurs in build_filter()
the filter chain will be freed by build_filter(). Next
the expectation is that execution proceeds to fz_catch()
where fz_drop_stream() would be called with chain == NULL.

However due to the chain variable residing in a register,
its value is not NULL as expected, but was reset to its
original value upon the exception (since they use setjmp()),
hence fz_drop_stream() is called with a non-NULL value.

Marking the chain variable with fz_var() prevents the
compiler from allowing the chain variable to reside in
a register and hence its value will remain NULL and
never be reset.

```c
	if (rc->uwbd.task == NULL)
		printk(KERN_ERR "UWB: Cannot start management daemon; "
		       "UWB won't work\n");
	else
		rc->uwbd.pid = rc->uwbd.task->pid;
```

Local operation causing UWB device initialization to fail.

The flaw is triggered when a USB audio device fails to probe successfully, leaving a URB (USB Request Block) active. static void snd_usb_mixer_free(struct usb_mixer_interface *mixer)
```c
{
	kfree(mixer->id_elems);
	if (mixer->urb) {
		kfree(mixer->urb->transfer_buffer);
		usb_free_urb(mixer->urb);
	}
	usb_free_urb(mixer->rc_urb);
	kfree(mixer->rc_setup_packet);
```

- The device is connected to the target system.
- The device's behavior triggers an error during the ALSA driver's probe phase.
- This causes the `snd_usb_mixer_free` function to be called, which frees the `mixer` object without cancelling the pending URB.

```c
	if (mixer->urb) {
		kfree(mixer->urb->transfer_buffer);
		usb_free_urb(mixer->urb);
	}
	usb_free_urb(mixer->rc_urb);
	kfree(mixer->rc_setup_packet);
	kfree(mixer);
```

Kernel USB driver (ALSA usb-audio)

```c
	return 0;
}
```

Kernel driver device unbinding

Use-after-free leading to arbitrary write

The Vulnerability
[Optional] CWE/CVE Number and description:

The bug is in the `snd_usb_create_streams` function within the Linux kernel's USB audio driver (`sound/usb/card.c`). The driver fails to properly validate the length of the descriptor (`h1->bLength`) and the number of interfaces it claims to contain (`h1->bInCollection`), leading to an out-of-bounds read when accessing the `baInterfaceNr` array in a loop, as shown in the code excerpt. [Mandatory] Root cause:
Unchecked buffer length and collection count fields from a device-supplied descriptor.
[Mandatory] Attack Surface:
USB audio device driver (physical access via malicious USB device).
[Mandatory] Impact Summary:
Local privilege escalation

```c
for (i = 0; i < h1->bInCollection; i++)
	snd_usb_create_stream(chip, ctrlif, h1->baInterfaceNr[i]);
```

[Mandatory] Trigger surface/attack vector:
USB device insertion (malicious audio device)

[Mandatory] Exploit primitive(s) available:
Out-of-bounds read

[Mandatory] Exploitability summary (1 sentence):
Exploitability is high for an attacker with physical access, as it simply requires connecting a specially crafted USB device to trigger the vulnerability.

- Craft a USB audio device with a UAC1 control interface descriptor.
- Set the `bInCollection` field to a large value.
- Set the `bLength` field to a value smaller than `sizeof(uac1_ac_header_descriptor) + bInCollection`.
- Connect the device to a target system.
- The kernel driver will read past the descriptor buffer when iterating through the `baInterfaceNr` array.
- This results in an out-of-bounds read of adjacent kernel memory.

Fix
[Mandatory] Fix code:
```c
rest_bytes = (void *)(host_iface->extra + host_iface->extralen) -
	control_header;

/* just to be sure -- this shouldn't hit at all */
if (rest_bytes <= 0) {
	dev_err(&dev->dev, "invalid control header\n");
	return -EINVAL;
}

if (rest_bytes < sizeof(*h1)) {
	dev_err(&dev->dev, "too short v1 buffer descriptor\n");
	return -EINVAL;
}

if (rest_bytes < h1->bLength) {
	dev_err(&dev->dev, "invalid buffer length (v1)\n");
	return -EINVAL;
}

if (h1->bLength < sizeof(*h1) + h1->bInCollection) {
	dev_err(&dev->dev, "invalid UAC_HEADER (v1)\n");
	return -EINVAL;
}
```
[Mandatory] Fix summary:
The patch adds multiple bounds checks on the device-supplied buffer descriptor. It calculates the remaining bytes (`rest_bytes`) and verifies that the descriptor is large enough to contain its header, the claimed total length (`bLength`), and the full list of interface numbers (`bInCollection`), preventing out-of-bounds reads.

The bug is in the `uas_switch_interface` function within the Linux kernel's UAS driver. {
```c
	int alt;

	alt = uas_find_uas_alt_setting(intf);
	if (alt < 0)
		return alt;

	return usb_set_interface(udev,
		intf->altsetting[0].desc.bInterfaceNumber, alt);
```

Malicious USB device

commit_message:
USB: uas: fix bug in handling of alternate settings

The uas driver has a subtle bug in the way it handles alternate
settings.  The uas_find_uas_alt_setting() routine returns an
altsetting value (the bAlternateSetting number in the descriptor), but
uas_use_uas_driver() then treats that value as an index to the
intf->altsetting array, which it isn't.

Normally this doesn't cause any problems because the various
alternate settings have bAlternateSetting values 0, 1, 2, ..., so the
value is equal to the index in the array.  But this is not guaranteed,
and Andrey Konovalov used the syzkaller fuzzer with KASAN to get a
slab-out-of-bounds error by violating this assumption.

This patch fixes the bug by making uas_find_uas_alt_setting() return a
pointer to the altsetting entry rather than either the value or the
index.  Pointers are less subject to misinterpretation.

The uas driver has a subtle bug in the way it handles alternate
settings.  The uas_find_uas_alt_setting() routine returns an
altsetting value (the bAlternateSetting number in the descriptor), but
uas_use_uas_driver() then treats that value as an index to the

pointer to the altsetting entry rather than either the value or the
index.  Pointers are less subject to misinterpretation.

descriptors for a device. If the received hid descriptor is smaller than

out-of-bounds.

value, this can also cause out-of-bounds while approaching hdesc->desc[n].

So check the size of hid descriptor and bNumDescriptors.

commit_message:
USB: core: fix out-of-bounds access bug in usb_get_bos_descriptor()

Andrey used the syzkaller fuzzer to find an out-of-bounds memory
access in usb_get_bos_descriptor().  The code wasn't checking that the
next usb_dev_cap_header structure could fit into the remaining buffer
space.

This patch fixes the error and also reduces the bNumDeviceCaps field
in the header to match the actual number of capabilities found, in
cases where there are fewer than expected.

The Vulnerability
[Optional] CWE/CVE Number and description:
Out-of-bounds read

[Mandatory] Summary:
The bug is in the read_header function of libavcodec/ffv1dec.c, where the loop condition for counting slices does not account for the variable trailer size when f->ec is set. This can cause p - c->bytestream_start to be insufficient, leading to an out-of-bounds read when accessing p-trailer. The vulnerability is exploitable because the loop may read beyond the bytestream buffer.

[Mandatory] Root cause:
Incorrect loop condition that does not include the variable trailer size in the boundary check.

Media parser (FFV1 decoder)

[Mandatory] Impact Summary:
Out-of-bounds read → potential information leak or crash

[Optional] Trigger / Attack vector:
Malformed FFV1 video bitstream

[Mandatory] Key code/struct excerpt (minimal):

    for (f->slice_count = 0;
         f->slice_count < MAX_SLICES && 3 < p - c->bytestream_start;
         f->slice_count++) {
        int trailer = 3 + 5*!!f->ec;
        int size = AV_RB24(p-trailer);
        if (size + trailer > p - c->bytestream_start)
            break;
        p -= size + trailer;
    }

Exploit:

[Mandatory] Trigger surface/attack vector:
FFV1 video file parsing

[Mandatory] Exploit primitive(s) available:
Out-of-bounds read

- Ensure the bytestream is short enough that 3 < p - c->bytestream_start passes but 3 + 5*!!f->ec does not.

- Observe out-of-bounds read behavior.

Fix
[Mandatory] Fix code:

    for (f->slice_count = 0;
         f->slice_count < MAX_SLICES && 3 + 5*!!f->ec < p - c->bytestream_start;
         f->slice_count++) {

        int size = AV_RB24(p-trailer);
        if (size + trailer > p - c->bytestream_start)
            break;
        p -= size + trailer;
    }

[Mandatory] Fix summary:
The patch updates the loop condition to include the variable trailer size (3 + 5*!!f->ec) in the boundary check, preventing out-of-bounds access.

sunrpc: Avoid use-after-free read access in clntudp_call [BZ #21115]

commit_message:
xen/mm: make sure node is less than MAX_NUMNODES

The output of MEMF_get_node(memflags) can be as large as nodeid_t can
hold (currently 255).  This is then used as an index to arrays of size
MAX_NUMNODE, which is 64 on x86 and 1 on ARM, can be passed in by an
untrusted guest (via memory_exchange and increase_reservation) and is
not currently bounds-checked.

Check the value in page_alloc.c before using it, and also check the
value in the hypercall call sites and return -EINVAL if appropriate.
Don't permit domains other than the hardware or control domain to
allocate node-constrained memory.

This is CVE-2017-14316 / XSA-231.

commit_message:
Preserve GSS context on init/accept failure

After gss_init_sec_context() or gss_accept_sec_context() has created a
context, don't delete the mechglue context on failures from subsequent
calls, even if the mechanism deletes the mech-specific context (which
is allowed by RFC 2744 but not preferred).  Check for union contexts
with no mechanism context in each GSS function which accepts a
gss_ctx_id_t.

CVE-2017-11462:

RFC 2744 permits a GSS-API implementation to delete an existing
security context on a second or subsequent call to

[Mandatory] Summary:
 The bug exists in the `gss_inquire_context` function within the MIT krb5 GSSAPI library. It is triggered when an attacker induces a GSSAPI call to fail after a security context has been established, causing the underlying mechanism to free its internal context while the mechglue wrapper retains a pointer to it. The gss_inquire_context API function.

Double free leading to memory corruption (potentially use-after-free or arbitrary write).

Preserve GSS context on init/accept failure

After gss_init_sec_context() or gss_accept_sec_context() has created a
context, don't delete the mechglue context on failures from subsequent
calls, even if the mechanism deletes the mech-specific context (which
is allowed by RFC 2744 but not preferred).  Check for union contexts
with no mechanism context in each GSS function which accepts a
gss_ctx_id_t.

security context on a second or subsequent call to
gss_init_sec_context() or gss_accept_sec_context() if the call results
in an error.  This API behavior has been found to be dangerous,
leading to the possibility of memory errors in some callers.  For
safety, GSS-API implementations should instead preserve existing
security contexts on error until the caller deletes them.

All versions of MIT krb5 prior to this change may delete acceptor
contexts on error.  Versions 1.13.4 through 1.13.7, 1.14.1 through
1.14.5, and 1.15 through 1.15.1 may also delete initiator contexts on
error.

The Vulnerability
[Optional] CWE/CVE Number and description:
